# Why the Roman Empire Fell

In the year 476, a teenage emperor named Romulus Augustulus handed over his crown to a Germanic general, and nobody even bothered to kill him. They sent him off to retire in southern Italy. So how did an empire that once ruled about 60 million people end with a shrug instead of a bang?

## It wasn't one bad day

Here's the first surprise: "Rome fell" mostly means the **western half** fell. By the late 300s, the empire was run as two halves. The <KeyTerm term="Western Roman Empire" definition="The western half of the empire, covering Italy, Gaul, Spain, Britain and North Africa. Its last emperor was removed in 476."/> was ruled from Italy. The eastern half was run from Constantinople, today's Istanbul. The East kept going for almost another thousand years.

The West fell apart slowly. The fall began in 410, when Rome was sacked by the Visigoths, a wandering Germanic people from the northeast.<Cite refs={["turn0search0"]}/> In 455 the Vandals sacked Rome too, and after that Italy's politics were unstable almost all the time.<Cite refs={["turn0search1"]}/>

By the time of the famous date, the Western emperor had almost no military, political or financial power left<Cite refs={["turn0search2"]}/>. People at the time didn't even think 476 was special: nine Western emperors had come and gone since 455, and barbarian commanders had overthrown most of them.<Cite refs={["turn0search3"]}/>

<Timeline title="The long fall of the West" events={[{"date":"235–284","label":"Crisis of the Third Century","description":"Civil wars, invasions and ruined money nearly break the empire."},{"date":"395","label":"The empire splits for good","description":"East and West get separate emperors."},{"date":"410","label":"Visigoths sack Rome","description":"The first time in 800 years that foreign enemies loot the city."},{"date":"439","label":"Vandals take Carthage","description":"The West loses its richest tax and grain province, North Africa."},{"date":"455","label":"Vandals sack Rome","description":"Emperors now rise and fall every few years."},{"date":"476","label":"Last Western emperor removed","description":"Odoacer retires Romulus Augustulus."},{"date":"1453","label":"The East falls","description":"Ottoman Turks capture Constantinople."}]}/>

<Callout title="Wonder lens" tone="insight">Historians call 476 a "convenient" date. It's like a funeral: it gives you a date to remember, but the illness had been going on for decades.</Callout>

dil.fallbackMarkdown:
# Why the Roman Empire Fell

In the year 476, a teenage emperor named Romulus Augustulus handed over his crown to a Germanic general, and nobody even bothered to kill him. They sent him off to retire in southern Italy. So how did an empire that once ruled about 60 million people end with a shrug instead of a bang?

## It wasn't one bad day

Here's the first surprise: "Rome fell" mostly means the **western half** fell. By the late 300s, the empire was run as two halves. The **Western Roman Empire** (The western half of the empire, covering Italy, Gaul, Spain, Britain and North Africa. Its last emperor was removed in 476.) was ruled from Italy. The eastern half was run from Constantinople, today's Istanbul. The East kept going for almost another thousand years.

The West fell apart slowly. The fall began in 410, when Rome was sacked by the Visigoths, a wandering Germanic people from the northeast. In 455 the Vandals sacked Rome too, and after that Italy's politics were unstable almost all the time.

By the time of the famous date, the Western emperor had almost no military, political or financial power left. People at the time didn't even think 476 was special: nine Western emperors had come and gone since 455, and barbarian commanders had overthrown most of them.

**The long fall of the West**

- 235–284 — **Crisis of the Third Century**: Civil wars, invasions and ruined money nearly break the empire.
- 395 — **The empire splits for good**: East and West get separate emperors.
- 410 — **Visigoths sack Rome**: The first time in 800 years that foreign enemies loot the city.
- 439 — **Vandals take Carthage**: The West loses its richest tax and grain province, North Africa.
- 455 — **Vandals sack Rome**: Emperors now rise and fall every few years.
- 476 — **Last Western emperor removed**: Odoacer retires Romulus Augustulus.
- 1453 — **The East falls**: Ottoman Turks capture Constantinople.

**Wonder lens** Historians call 476 a "convenient" date. It's like a funeral: it gives you a date to remember, but the illness had been going on for decades.

## Problem 1: The money went bad

Rome paid its soldiers in silver coins. The main coin was the **denarius** (Rome's everyday silver coin. Soldiers were paid in it.).

At first, the coin was almost pure silver. Under Augustus, it was around 95-98% silver.

But the army kept growing. Emperors needed more coins. They didn't have more silver. So they cheated. They mixed in cheap metal. This is called **debasement** (Putting less gold or silver into a coin while still saying it's worth the same.).

It got worse over time. Around the year 200, the coin was only about 40-50% silver. By 270, it was mostly cheap metal with a thin silver coating.

People noticed. Once they realized the coins held much less silver than they claimed, prices shot up out of control. A soldier's pay bought less and less. Unhappy soldiers are dangerous soldiers.

**How much silver was in Rome's coin?**

- **Augustus (~1 AD)** (96 % silver)
- **Nero (~65 AD)** (92 % silver)
- **Marcus Aurelius (~170)** (70 % silver)
- **Caracalla (~215)** (50 % silver)
- **Around 270**: Basically a copper coin wearing a silver coat. (4 % silver)

**Think of it like this** Imagine your $10 bill slowly turns into $1 worth of paper. The number on it stays the same, but the shop prices keep going up.

## Problem 2: Too many enemies at once

Rome's borders were very long. They ran thousands of kilometers. Soldiers had to guard all of it.

Then a new danger arrived from the east: the **Huns** (Fierce horse-riding warriors from Central Asia who pushed into Europe in the late 300s.). The Huns didn't attack Rome first. They attacked other peoples. Those peoples ran away, straight toward Rome.

One push led to the next, like dominoes. Step through the chain below.

**The domino chain: from the Huns to the sack of Rome**

- **1. The Huns arrive (about 370)**: Horse warriors from Central Asia attack the Goths living north of the Black Sea.
- **2. The Goths flee (376)**: Tens of thousands of Goths ask to cross the Danube River into Roman land. Rome lets them in.
- **3. Things go wrong**: Roman officials treat the Goths badly. They sell them food at terrible prices. The Goths get angry and fight back.
- **4. A huge Roman defeat (378)**: At the Battle of Adrianople, the Goths crush a Roman army. The emperor Valens is killed.
- **5. Goths inside the empire**: Rome can't drive them out. Now a whole armed people lives inside the borders.
- **6. Rome is sacked (410)**: The Visigoths, led by Alaric, march into Italy and loot the city of Rome.

## Problem 3: Many cracks, one collapse

So which problem killed Rome? The honest answer: all of them, together.

Each problem made the others worse. Bad money made soldiers unhappy. Unhappy soldiers backed rival generals. Generals fought **civil war** (A war between groups inside the same country, instead of against an outside enemy.)s for the throne. While Romans fought Romans, the borders were left weak. Invaders got in. They took rich land. Less land meant fewer taxes. Fewer taxes meant even less money for the army.

That's a loop. It kept spinning, faster and faster.

Why did the East survive? It was richer. It had more cities and more taxes. And its capital, Constantinople, had huge walls and sat behind the sea.

**Rome's downward spiral**

- **Money runs short**: Coins lose silver. Prices rise.
- **Army gets unhappy**: Soldiers back generals who promise more pay.
- **Civil wars**: Romans fight Romans for the throne.
- **Borders weaken**: Invaders get in more easily.
- **Land and taxes lost**: Fewer taxes mean even less money.

**Explain it back:** In your own words, why do historians say Rome fell from many causes working together, not just one?

## Check your understanding

**Check your understanding**

1. What does 'Rome fell in 476' really mean?
- The whole empire disappeared in one day
- The western half lost its last emperor, while the eastern half kept going
- The city of Rome was destroyed by fire
2. Emperors put less silver in coins but said the coins were worth the same. What happened?
- Prices went up and soldiers' pay bought less
- Rome became richer
- Nothing changed, because nobody noticed
3. True or false: The Huns started the chain that brought the Goths into the Roman Empire.
- True
- False
